summaries.gardner: Disney has some Rule Breaker traits, including a world-famous brand, a lasting edge in characters and parks, and strong pricing power. But it is a 100-year-old incumbent in mature markets rather than the leader of an emerging industry, and its shares have lagged badly, roughly flat over the past year and about 35% below October 2021 levels. That makes it a poor fit for Gardner's top-dog-and-momentum approach.
summaries.buffett: Disney has the kind of durable, hard-to-copy franchise Buffett likes, since its characters, parks and brand earn money again and again, and the business is simple to understand. Against that, returns on capital are modest (about 6-7% after tax on invested capital, weighed down by $74.7bn of goodwill from acquisitions), net debt is about $41bn, results were patchy from 2020 to 2023, and past acquisitions such as 21st Century Fox have not clearly paid off. It fits partly: a wonderful brand at a fair price (about 16 times forward earnings), but not an obvious Buffett-quality compounder.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the cross-selling flywheel that runs from films to parks, merchandise and streaming, but would note how many ways the business can stumble: cord-cutting, sports-rights inflation, creative misses and capital-heavy parks. Thinking backwards, the IP and parks are very hard to destroy, but heavy reinvestment needs and a history of overpaying for deals make it a less clear-cut 'great business at a fair price'.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms Disney is a stalwart-turnaround hybrid: earnings are recovering strongly (adjusted EPS guided up about 16% in FY2026 including the 53rd week) after the 2020-2023 slump, with a simple story of parks plus profitable streaming. The forward P/E of about 15-16 is roughly twice its expected EPS growth of about 8% for FY2027, though buybacks are cutting the share count and a director bought shares in February 2026.
summaries.fisher: Disney scores well on Fisher's sales, marketing and product-development points: it is unusually good at selling and keeps renewing its franchises with films, rides and cruise ships. Its margins have improved since FY2021 (segment margin up to 18.6% in FY2025), but creative execution has been uneven (several 2026 live-action misses) and leadership has just changed. It is a partial fit for Fisher's long-term growth approach.
summaries.graham: Disney fails most of Graham's defensive tests. It made a net loss in FY2020, suspended its dividend from 2020 to 2023, trades at about 31 times its three-year average EPS and has a P/E times P/B of about 40, far above 22.5. Only its size and its roughly 40% ten-year EPS growth pass.
summaries.thiel: Disney is a durable near-monopoly in owned characters and destination parks, with excellent distribution, but it is not built on proprietary technology ten times better than rivals, and its main markets are mature. It answers Thiel's durability and distribution questions well, but the technology, timing and secret questions poorly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on growth plus efficiency, the Rule of 40 and getting fit. Disney has done the cost-cutting, with streaming profit more than doubling and margins rising, but revenue growth of about 6-7% and an FCF margin of about 8-11% sum to well under 40. The stock suits a value or turnaround argument more than Gerstner's high-growth-at-reasonable-price lens.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and upward estimate revisions with a catalyst. Disney has some of this: three straight quarterly beats in FY2026, rising guidance ($9bn of buybacks, about 16% adjusted EPS growth) and a new CEO. But the share price has not confirmed it (about +1.5% over the last year against about +16% for the S&P 500), and the business is sensitive to consumer spending and travel.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high gross margins and cash conversion at a fair price. Disney's gross margin of about 38%, ROIC in the mid-single digits, heavy capex (about $9bn guided for FY2026) and acquisition-driven goodwill fall short of Fundsmith-style quality, even though the brand is excellent. It is not a natural fit.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Disney's earnings yield (segment operating income about $18.2bn over the last twelve months, against an enterprise value of about $232bn, or about 7.9%) is moderate. Its return on tangible capital is diluted by large parks investment, so it would likely rank mid-pack rather than near the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented and honest management, and high-return reinvestment. Disney's business leg is strong, but the management leg is unproven after the March 2026 CEO change, and the reinvestment leg (about $8-9bn a year into parks and cruises, with double-digit lifetime returns targeted) earns returns only a little above Disney's cost of capital so far. It is a partial fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai wants low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at big discounts. Disney's permanent-loss risk is low given its IP, parks and $110bn of equity, and it has worked through a temporary setback (streaming losses, linear decline, succession turmoil). But at about 16 times forward earnings it is not trading at the deep discount Dhandho requires.
summaries.wood: Disney is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense. It is an incumbent being disrupted by streaming and short-form video, though its $1bn OpenAI deal, Epic Games stake and Disney+ push show it is adapting. It does not fit Cathie Wood's framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and limited outside risks. Disney's iconic brand, about $10bn of FY2025 free cash flow and buybacks fit, but its sensitivity to consumer spending, sports-rights costs and cord-cutting reduces predictability. A management transition or turnaround angle could appeal.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for 'scale economies shared' businesses that pass savings back to customers. Disney does the opposite, raising prices for parks and Disney+ (for example Premium from $15.99 to $18.99 in October 2025), so it is a weak fit despite its durable brand.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products that solve big problems at the right time. Disney is a mature, diversified entertainment company, so his venture-style questions about a large painful problem and a new market fit poorly, though its markets are certainly large.
summaries.nash: Disney fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue grows about 6-7% a year, debt ($46.0bn) far exceeds cash ($5.2bn), the operating margin is below 20% and the shares have badly lagged the S&P 500 over five years. On a Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount it is worth about $38 a share against a price of about $111. Its strengths are the brand, consistent earnings beats and buybacks, but it scores about 70 of 130 on his categories, below the 75 threshold.

momentum.evidence: DIS traded at $110.60 in mid-October 2026, against a 52-week opening price of $109.00 (about +1.5%), while SPY rose about 16% over the same period.

g4.evidence: New CEO Josh D'Amaro built a strong record running Disney Experiences, and Disney has big-name partners in the NFL (10% of ESPN since early 2026), OpenAI and Epic Games, but the leadership team is newly reshaped after a long succession saga.

g6.evidence: At about 16 times FY2026 consensus adjusted EPS of $6.93, Disney is generally described as reasonably valued or cheap rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: Disney makes money from theme parks, streaming, ESPN, TV channels and films, which any careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Disney was consistently profitable for decades but posted a $2.9bn net loss in FY2020 and weak FY2021-FY2023 earnings (diluted EPS of $1.29 in FY2023) before recovering to $6.85 in FY2025.

integrity.evidence: Disney is candid in its disclosures and has returned capital through dividends and buybacks, but it faced years of succession turmoil (Chapek ousted in 2022, Iger extended twice), shareholder fights with Trian and Blackwells in 2024, and criticism of high executive pay.

b6.evidence: Recent management has focused on its core (selling its A+E stake for $1.2bn in 2026 and merging Hulu Live with Fubo), but Disney's $71bn Fox acquisition in 2019 was empire-building whose returns remain doubtful.

roic.evidence: After-tax operating return on invested capital is about 6-7% (about $13.0bn FY2025 operating income against about $158bn of equity plus net debt), weighed down by $74.7bn of goodwill.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $10.1bn against $12.4bn of net income attributable to Disney, flattered by tax benefits; nine-month FY2026 free cash flow fell 24% to $5.7bn as capex rose.

b10.evidence: Disney's market value is well below its 2021 levels (shares down about 35% from October 2021) despite heavy reinvestment and acquisitions, so retained earnings have not created matching value.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF using 3-year average growth (4.5%) and FCF margin (8.5%) gives about $38-59 a share at 10-12% discount rates, well below the $110.60 price.

fairprice.evidence: About 16 times FY2026 and 15 times FY2027 consensus adjusted EPS ($6.93 and $7.47), with a free-cash-flow yield of about 4.3% on trailing twelve months, is reasonable for a business with brand quality but mid-single-digit revenue growth.

mu5.evidence: The IP library and parks are very hard to destroy, but cord-cutting, sports-rights inflation, a consumer downturn and creative misses are several plausible ways for profits to erode.

reinvest.evidence: Disney plans about $9bn of FY2026 capex, largely parks and cruise ships, and targets double-digit lifetime returns on major expansions, but company-wide returns on capital are only mid-single digits.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart and turnaround: parks plus a now-profitable streaming business (Q3 FY2026 streaming operating income $712m, up from $329m) driving double-digit EPS growth.

ly3.evidence: A forward P/E of about 14.8 on FY2027 estimates is roughly double the expected 7.8% EPS growth from $6.93 to $7.47.

runway.evidence: Growth avenues include a planned Abu Dhabi park, more cruise ships, ESPN streaming and international Disney+, but consensus sees only about 5-6% annual revenue growth through FY2028.

ly7.evidence: Director Amy Chang bought 916 shares at $107.85 in February 2026 and diluted shares fell from 1,811m in FY2025 to 1,743m in Q3 FY2026 on $7.2bn of nine-month buybacks, though other insiders have sold small amounts.

ly8.evidence: Disney is one of the most widely covered stocks, with about 29 analysts estimating its FY2026 revenue.

fi2.evidence: Disney keeps launching new products as old ones mature, including the ESPN streaming app (2025), new cruise ships (Disney Destiny and Disney Adventure), new park lands and a Disney+ push to become 'the digital centerpiece' of the company.

fi3.evidence: Content and Imagineering spending produces hits like Toy Story 5 (over $1bn at the box office in 2026) and record parks income, but 2026 live-action films such as Moana and The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed.

fi4.evidence: Disney is a marketing powerhouse that cross-sells each franchise through films, streaming, parks and merchandise, and raised Disney+ prices in October 2025 while growing subscription revenue 15%.

longterm.evidence: Disney keeps investing heavily in long-lived assets (about $9bn of FY2026 capex and a 10-year, $60bn Experiences investment plan announced in 2023) but has also made deep cost cuts and leaned on buybacks to hit EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: Disney had $94.4bn of FY2025 revenue and a market value of about $191bn.

ni10.evidence: Disney reported a net loss attributable to Disney of $2,864m in FY2020.

gr4.evidence: Disney suspended its dividend in 2020 and paid none in FY2021-FY2023 (zero dividends in the FY2023 cash flow statement) before reinstating it in 2024.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $4.90 in FY2015 to $6.85 in FY2025 (+40%), though FY2025 was lifted by a $1.4bn income-tax benefit.

gr6.evidence: The $110.60 price is about 31 times average diluted EPS for FY2023-FY2025 ($3.62).

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 22.8 (TTM diluted EPS $4.85) times a P/B of about 1.74 gives about 40, well above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Disney's advantage is owned IP and experiences, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Streaming has reached profitability (SVOD margins guided to double digits in FY2026) and parks demand is solid, but linear TV is declining and AI video is a new risk.

th3.evidence: Disney started as an animation studio in 1923 and has long since expanded into large, mature global markets, so this start-up question no longer applies.

team.evidence: CEO Josh D'Amaro (since March 2026) and President and Chief Creative Officer Dana Walden are respected operators, but the team is newly formed and unproven at the top.

th5.evidence: Disney owns its distribution through Disney+, Hulu, ESPN, ABC and its parks, giving direct access to hundreds of millions of customers.

durable.evidence: Characters such as Mickey, Marvel and Star Wars and destination parks like Walt Disney World have stayed popular for decades and should still matter in 10-20 years, even if linear TV fades.

th7.evidence: Disney's opportunities (parks expansion, streaming, ESPN direct-to-consumer) are well known to rivals and investors.

trend.evidence: Disney is adapting to the streaming shift and has partnered with OpenAI on AI video, but it is not a leading beneficiary of AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Q3 FY2026 adjusted EPS rose 28% to $2.06 against a $1.88 consensus, and Disney raised its FY2026 outlook to about 16% adjusted EPS growth including the 53rd week, with at least $9bn of buybacks.

dr2.evidence: Rising streaming margins, new cruise ships and park expansions could improve results by 2028, but much of this is already guided and expected.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates would help a company with $46.0bn of borrowings and capital-heavy parks, but parks depend on consumer spending, and Disney cited weak international visits to US parks in 2026.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include FY2026 results in November 2026 with FY2027 guidance (double-digit adjusted EPS growth targeted), the closing of the $1.2bn A+E stake sale and new cruise ships and park openings.

dr7.evidence: Weak share-price momentum, mid-single-digit revenue growth and a new CEO make Disney hard to justify as a large concentrated position under this style.

gm.evidence: FY2025 gross margin, after the cost of services and products, was about 37.8% ($35.7bn on $94.4bn), moderate rather than high.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow of about $8.3bn is a 4.3% yield on a roughly $191bn market value (5.3% on FY2025 FCF of $10.1bn), reasonable but not cheap given slow growth.

gb2.evidence: Trailing segment operating income of about $18.2bn is about 7.9% of an enterprise value near $232bn (about 5.6% using FY2025 GAAP operating income of about $13.0bn), a middling figure.

pa2.evidence: Streaming losses and the succession saga have been largely fixed (streaming is now profitable and a new CEO is in place), but linear TV decline is structural rather than temporary.

pa4.evidence: Permanent loss looks unlikely given Disney's irreplaceable IP and parks, $110.0bn of shareholders' equity and positive free cash flow every year since FY2020.

wo1.evidence: Disney is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing, though it uses robotics in parks and licenses characters to OpenAI's Sora.

wo2.evidence: Its costs (content, sports rights, park construction) are rising, not falling sharply with volume.

wo3.evidence: Disney does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Disney's addressable markets are large but mature; consensus expects revenue to grow only to about $110bn by FY2028 from $94.4bn in FY2025.

ac3.evidence: Disney is insulated from commodity prices, but its parks and advertising are sensitive to the economy, travel and consumer confidence, and it carries $46.0bn of debt.

ns1.evidence: Disney uses its scale to raise prices (Disney+ Premium up from $15.99 to $18.99 in October 2025; per-guest park ticket revenue up 5% in Q3 FY2026) rather than passing savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Parks and IP should be stronger in 10-20 years, but the TV and sports businesses face structural pressure, so the overall position is not clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: Disney provides entertainment and family experiences, which are valued but do not cure a large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: Disney is an established media and parks business adapting to streaming, not a company built for a secular infrastructure trend like AI or energy.
